claim: The X-linked MIR-506 family miRNAs are located in a region flanked by two highly conserved protein-coding genes (SLITRK2 and FMR1) on the X chromosome.
source: Despite rapid evolution across eutherian mammals, the X-linked MIR-506 family miRNAs are located in a region flanked by two highly conserved protein-coding genes (SLITRK2 and FMR1) on the X chromosome.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by genomic location data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The X-linked MIR-506 family miRNAs are predominantly expressed in the testis.
source: Intriguingly, these miRNAs are predominantly expressed in the testis, suggesting a potential role in spermatogenesis and male fertility.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by expression data from multiple species shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The X-linked MIR-506 family miRNAs were derived from the MER91C DNA transposons.
source: Here, we report that the X-linked MIR-506 family miRNAs were derived from the MER91C DNA transposons.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 2A, phylogenetic analysis in Figure 2B, and experimental validation in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Selective inactivation of individual miRNAs or clusters caused no discernible defects.
source: Selective inactivation of individual miRNAs or clusters caused no discernible defects, but simultaneous ablation of five clusters containing 19 members of the MIR-506 family led to reduced male fertility in mice.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing no phenotypic changes in single and double knockout mice (Figure 4B-C).

claim: Simultaneous ablation of five clusters containing 19 members of the MIR-506 family led to reduced male fertility in mice.
source: Selective inactivation of individual miRNAs or clusters caused no discernible defects, but simultaneous ablation of five clusters containing 19 members of the MIR-506 family led to reduced male fertility in mice.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by litter size data in Figure 4B showing significantly smaller litters in quinKO males.

claim: The quinKO sperm had normal sperm counts, motility, and morphology.
source: Despite normal sperm counts, motility, and morphology, the KO sperm were less competitive than wild-type sperm when subjected to a polyandrous mating scheme.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by CASA data in Figure 4E-F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H showing no significant differences.

claim: The quinKO sperm were less competitive than wild-type sperm when subjected to a polyandrous mating scheme.
source: Despite normal sperm counts, motility, and morphology, the KO sperm were less competitive than wild-type sperm when subjected to a polyandrous mating scheme.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by sequential mating experiments (Figure 4H-I), IVF experiments (Figure 4J), and co-artificial insemination experiments (Figure 4K).

claim: The X-linked MIR-506 family miRNAs have more targets that are critical for spermatogenesis and embryonic development during evolution.
source: Transcriptomic and bioinformatic analyses revealed that these X-linked MIR-506 family miRNAs, in addition to targeting a set of conserved genes, have more targets that are critical for spermatogenesis and embryonic development during evolution.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by comparative analysis showing human MIR-506 family members target more genes per miRNA than mouse counterparts (Figure 6F).

claim: The MIR-506 family miRNAs function to enhance sperm competitiveness and reproductive fitness of the male by finetuning gene expression during spermatogenesis.
source: Our data suggest that the MIR-506 family miRNAs function to enhance sperm competitiveness and reproductive fitness of the male by finetuning gene expression during spermatogenesis.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the combination of reduced sperm competitiveness in quinKO mice and the identification of target genes involved in spermatogenesis.

claim: SLITRK2 and FMR1 mapped to chromosome 4 in zebrafish and birds, but to the X chromosome in most mammals.
source: Through tracing the evolution of this genomic region, we found that SLITRK2 and FMR1 mapped to chromosome 4 (syntenic with mammalian X chromosome) in zebrafish and birds, but to the X chromosome in most mammals, with divergence and multiplication of numerous miRNA genes that belong to the MIR-506 family in between (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by genomic location data shown in Figure 1A across multiple species.

claim: All members of the MIR-506 family are located in a region flanked by SLITRK2 and FMR1.
source: By mapping these miRNAs of various species using the UCSC genome browser (Casper et al., 2018), we found that all members of the MIR-506 family are located in a region flanked by SLITRK2 and FMR1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by genomic mapping data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SLITRK2 and FMR1 are usually on the positive strand, whereas the MIR-506 family miRNAs are in the reverse orientation.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Wang et al., 2020b; Zhang et al., 2019), SLITRK2 and FMR1 are usually on the positive strand, whereas the MIR-506 family miRNAs are in the reverse orientation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations to previous reports and supported by genomic orientation data in Figure 1A.

claim: The mean values of PhyloP and PhastCons of the FMR1 and SLITRK2 coding sequences were ~4.9 and ~0.97, respectively.
source: The mean values of PhyloP and PhastCons of the FMR1 and SLITRK2 coding sequences (CDS) were ~4.9 and ~0.97, respectively (Figure 1C and D), indicating that these regions are highly conserved.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by conservation score data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The mean values of PhyloP and PhastCons of SmiRs were ~1.0 and ~0.002, respectively.
source: In contrast, the mean values of PhyloP and PhastCons of SmiRs were ~1.0 and ~0.002, respectively, and those of FmiRs are ~0.03 and ~0.11, respectively (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by conservation score data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The mean values of PhyloP and PhastCons of FmiRs are ~0.03 and ~0.11, respectively.
source: In contrast, the mean values of PhyloP and PhastCons of SmiRs were ~1.0 and ~0.002, respectively, and those of FmiRs are ~0.03 and ~0.11, respectively (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by conservation score data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: FmiRs and SmiRs are highly divergent, and SmiRs are more divergent than FmiRs.
source: The PhyloP and PhastCons values of the CDS, FmiRs, and SmiRs are significantly different from each other (adjusted p-value <0.05, Kruskal–Wallis test) (Figure 1C and D), indicating that FmiRs and SmiRs are highly divergent, and SmiRs are more divergent than FmiRs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by statistical comparison of conservation scores shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The SLITRK2-FMR1 genomic regions were highly variable among different species.
source: Although the SLITRK2-FMR1 genomic regions were highly variable among different species, the sequences within some clades shared a high degree of similarities, for example, primates (rhesus monkeys, chimpanzees, and humans), cetartiodactyla (sheep and cows), rodentia (e.g., mice and rats), and carnivora (e.g., dogs and cats) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by D-GENIES-based dot plot analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The sequences within some clades shared a high degree of similarities, for example, primates, cetartiodactyla, rodentia, and carnivora.
source: Although the SLITRK2-FMR1 genomic regions were highly variable among different species, the sequences within some clades shared a high degree of similarities, for example, primates (rhesus monkeys, chimpanzees, and humans), cetartiodactyla (sheep and cows), rodentia (e.g., mice and rats), and carnivora (e.g., dogs and cats) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by D-GENIES-based dot plot analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The majority of the substitutions among the MIR-506 family are U→C and A→G.
source: It is noteworthy that the majority of the substitutions among the MIR-506 family are U→C and A→G (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: The DAF and MND of FmiRs and all miRNAs were significantly smaller than that of the pachytene piRNAs.
source: Of interest, the derived allele frequency (DAF) and mean nucleotide diversity (MND) of FmiRs and all miRNAs were significantly smaller than that of the pachytene piRNAs, whereas SmiRs were significantly smaller than all miRNAs (Figure 1E and F) (adjusted p-value<0.05, Kruskal–Wallis test), suggesting that the MIR-506 family miRNAs are more conserved than pachytene piRNAs in modern humans.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by statistical analysis of 1000 Genomes Project data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: SmiRs were significantly smaller than all miRNAs in terms of DAF and MND.
source: Of interest, the derived allele frequency (DAF) and mean nucleotide diversity (MND) of FmiRs and all miRNAs were significantly smaller than that of the pachytene piRNAs, whereas SmiRs were significantly smaller than all miRNAs (Figure 1E and F) (adjusted p-value<0.05, Kruskal–Wallis test), suggesting that the MIR-506 family miRNAs are more conserved than pachytene piRNAs in modern humans.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by statistical analysis of 1000 Genomes Project data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The MIR-506 family miRNAs are more conserved than pachytene piRNAs in modern humans.
source: Of interest, the derived allele frequency (DAF) and mean nucleotide diversity (MND) of FmiRs and all miRNAs were significantly smaller than that of the pachytene piRNAs, whereas SmiRs were significantly smaller than all miRNAs (Figure 1E and F) (adjusted p-value<0.05, Kruskal–Wallis test), suggesting that the MIR-506 family miRNAs are more conserved than pachytene piRNAs in modern humans.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by statistical analysis of 1000 Genomes Project data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The phylogram suggests that these miRNAs shared a common ancestor and that the FmiRs emerged earlier than the SmiRs.
source: The phylogram suggests that these miRNAs shared a common ancestor and that the FmiRs emerged earlier than the SmiRs, which is also supported by the fact that some FmiRs exist in green sea turtles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and presence of FmiRs in green sea turtles shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MIR-506 family miRNAs arose much earlier than previously thought.
source: These data suggest that the MIR-506 family miRNAs arose much earlier than previously thought (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by the presence of FmiRs in green sea turtles and phylogenetic analysis, contrasting with previous reports.

claim: The nonautonomous MER91C DNA transposon was the only transposon that aligned to FmiRs of the MIR-506 family in all four species analyzed.
source: The nonautonomous MER91C DNA transposon (~100–150 million years) (Giordano et al., 2007; Pace and Feschotte, 2007) was the only transposon that aligned to FmiRs of the MIR-506 family (>94% identical matches) in all four species (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations and supported by BLAST alignment results across human, horse, dog, and guinea pig genomes.

claim: Numerous FmiRs of almost all species analyzed aligned to the MER91C DNA transposon despite few mismatches.
source: Indeed, numerous FmiRs of almost all species analyzed aligned to the MER91C DNA transposon despite few mismatches (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The phylogenetic tree confirmed that the MER91C is the sister group of the MIR-506 family miRNAs.
source: The phylogenetic tree further confirmed that the MER91C is the sister group of the MIR-506 family miRNAs (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the MER91C DNA transposon is the likely source of the older MIR-506 family miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The MER91C DNA transposons could form hairpin structures, which is a prerequisite for miRNA biogenesis.
source: Further supporting this notion, the MER91C DNA transposons could form hairpin structures, which is a prerequisite for miRNA biogenesis (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by RNA structure prediction data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Analyses of the testis small RNA datasets from humans, marmosets, dogs, and horses revealed the peaks corresponding to these miRNAs.
source: Moreover, analyses of the testis small RNA datasets from humans, marmosets, dogs, and horses revealed the peaks corresponding to these miRNAs (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: MER91C DNA regions were capable of producing miRNAs when overexpressed in HEK293T cells.
source: Finally, by overexpressing several MER91C DNA regions randomly selected from humans, dogs, and horses in HEK293T cells, we found that these DNA regions were indeed capable of producing miRNAs (Figure 2E and F, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data from overexpression experiments shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Co-expression of MER91C DNA regions and AGO2 significantly increased the abundance of human MER91C miRNAs, as compared with overexpression of MER91C DNA regions alone.
source: Co-expression of MER91C DNA regions and AGO2 significantly increased the abundance of human MER91C miRNAs, as compared with overexpression of MER91C DNA regions alone (Figure 2E and F, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2), suggesting that these miRNAs could be loaded onto and protected by AGO2.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The X-linked MIR-506 family miRNAs were originally derived from the MER91C DNA transposon.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the X-linked MIR-506 family miRNAs were originally derived from the MER91C DNA transposon.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text as a conclusion from multiple lines of evidence including sequence alignment, phylogenetic analysis, and functional validation.

claim: MIR-506 family miRNAs were indeed highly abundant in the testis, but barely expressed in other organs.
source: By analyzing the publicly available small RNA sequencing (sRNA-seq) datasets from multiple species, including humans, rhesus monkeys, mice, rats, rabbits, dogs, and cows (Fromm et al., 2020; Keller et al., 2022; Bushel et al., 2020), we further confirmed that MIR-506 family miRNAs were indeed highly abundant in the testis, but barely expressed in other organs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations and supported by small RNA sequencing data from multiple species shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: These miRNAs were abundantly expressed in spermatogenic cells in murine testes.
source: Consistent with previous data (Wang et al., 2020b; Song et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2019), these miRNAs were abundantly expressed in spermatogenic cells in murine testes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations and supported by small RNA sequencing data from purified mouse spermatogenic cells shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Approximately 80% of these miRNAs were significantly upregulated when pachytene spermatocytes developed into round spermatids.
source: Approximately 80% of these miRNAs were significantly upregulated (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05) when pachytene spermatocytes developed into round spermatids, and ~83.3% were significantly upregulated (FDR < 0.05) when developed into cauda sperm (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Approximately 83.3% of these miRNAs were significantly upregulated when pachytene spermatocytes developed into cauda sperm.
source: Approximately 80% of these miRNAs were significantly upregulated (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05) when pachytene spermatocytes developed into round spermatids, and ~83.3% were significantly upregulated (FDR < 0.05) when developed into cauda sperm (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The MIR-506 family miRNAs are abundant in the testis and predominantly expressed in haploid male germ cells, that is, spermatids and spermatozoa.
source: Overall, the MIR-506 family miRNAs are abundant in the testis and predominantly expressed in haploid male germ cells, that is, spermatids and spermatozoa.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text as a summary of expression data from multiple species and cell types.

claim: The litter size was comparable between the tKO and WT control mice.
source: While the litter size was still comparable between the tKO and WT control mice, the quadKO, quinKO, and XS males produced significantly smaller litters (~5 vs. ~8 pups/litter) (adjusted p-value<0.05, one-way ANOVA) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by litter size data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The quadKO, quinKO, and XS males produced significantly smaller litters (~5 vs. ~8 pups/litter).
source: While the litter size was still comparable between the tKO and WT control mice, the quadKO, quinKO, and XS males produced significantly smaller litters (~5 vs. ~8 pups/litter) (adjusted p-value<0.05, one-way ANOVA) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by litter size data shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis.

claim: No significant changes were detected in litter interval, testis weight, or histology in any of the four types of KOs, as compared to WT controls.
source: Of interest, no significant changes were detected in litter interval, testis weight, or histology in any of the four types of KOs, as compared to WT controls (Figure 4C–G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4C-G.

claim: Computer-assisted sperm analyses revealed no significant differences in sperm counts and motility parameters among the four types of KOs.
source: Computer-assisted sperm analyses (CASA) revealed no significant differences in sperm counts and motility parameters among the four types of KOs (Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by CASA data shown in Figure 4E and F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: There appears to be an inverse correlation between the number of miRNAs inactivated and the litter size.
source: Overall, there appears to be an inverse correlation (R2 = 0.9139, p<0.05, F-test) between the number of miRNAs inactivated and the litter size (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Several human studies have correlated the dysregulated MIR-506 family miRNAs with impaired male fertility due to maturation arrest and oligo-asthenozoospermia.
source: Interestingly, several human studies have correlated the dysregulated MIR-506 family miRNAs with impaired male fertility due to maturation arrest and oligo-asthenozoospermia (Supplementary file 4; Abu-Halima et al., 2013; Heidary et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2018; Qing et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with multiple citations to human studies.

claim: All of the pups born were fathered by mTmG males when the WT females were mated first with mTmG males and subsequently with the quinKO males.
source: Interestingly, all of the pups born were fathered by mTmG males (n = 8) when the WT females were mated first with mTmG males and subsequently with the quinKO males.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by sequential mating experiment results shown in Figure 4H and I.

claim: When the WT females were mated first with quinKO males and subsequently with mTmG males, ~89% of the pups born were fathered by quinKO males, and the remaining ~11% of pups were from mTmG males.
source: In contrast, when the WT females were mated first with quinKO males and subsequently with mTmG males, ~89% of the pups born were fathered by quinKO males, and the remaining ~11% of pups were from mTmG males (n = 28) (Figure 4H and I, Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by sequential mating experiment results shown in Figure 4H and I.

claim: When a 1:1 ratio (mTmG sperm:quinKO sperm) was used in IVF, ~73% of the resulting blastocysts were derived from mTmG sperm, whereas the remaining ~27% were from quinKO sperm.
source: Interestingly, when a 1:1 ratio (mTmG sperm:quinKO sperm) was used, ~73% of the resulting blastocysts were derived from mTmG sperm, whereas the remaining ~27% were from quinKO sperm (n = 179) (p<0.0001, chi-squared test) (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by IVF experiment results shown in Figure 4J with statistical analysis.

claim: When a 4:1 sperm ratio (mTmG: quinKO) was used in IVF, ~92% of the blastocysts were from mTmG sperm and only 8% were from quinKO sperm.
source: When a 4:1 sperm ratio (mTmG: quinKO) was used, ~92% of the blastocysts were from mTmG sperm and only 8% were from quinKO sperm (n = 170) (p<0.05, chi-squared test) (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by IVF experiment results shown in Figure 4J with statistical analysis.

claim: When a 1:4 sperm ratio (mTmG:quinKO) was used in IVF, blastocysts derived from mTmG and quinKO sperm represented ~28% and ~72% of the total, respectively.
source: In contrast, when a 1:4 sperm ratio (mTmG:quinKO) was used, blastocysts derived from mTmG and quinKO sperm represented ~28% and ~72% of the total, respectively (n = 135) (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by IVF experiment results shown in Figure 4J.

claim: When a 1:1 sperm ratio (mTmG:quinKO) was used in co-artificial insemination, ~62.5% of the embryos were derived from mTmG sperm.
source: When a 1:1 sperm ratio (mTmG:quinKO) was used, ~62.5% of the embryos (n = 96) were derived from mTmG sperm (p<0.05, chi-squared test) (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by co-artificial insemination experiment results shown in Figure 4K with statistical analysis.

claim: When a 1:4 ratio was used in co-artificial insemination, ~35.3% of the embryos were from the mTmG mice.
source: When a 1:4 ratio was used, ~35.3% of the embryos (n = 17) were from the mTmG mice (Figure 4K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by co-artificial insemination experiment results shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The quinKO sperm are less competitive than the control mTmG sperm both in vivo and in vitro.
source: Together, these results indicate that the quinKO sperm are less competitive than the control mTmG sperm both in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text as a conclusion from sequential mating, IVF, and co-artificial insemination experiments.

claim: No changes in sperm aggregation and midpiece size were observed in the quinKO sperm.
source: Previous studies suggest that sperm aggregation and midpiece size might be involved in sperm competitiveness (Fisher and Hoekstra, 2010; Fisher et al., 2016), but no changes in these two parameters were observed in the quinKO sperm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K and L).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: The blastocyst rate of quinKO was comparable to that of the mTmG mice.
source: Although the blastocyst rate (out of two-cell embryos) of quinKO was comparable to that of the mTmG mice, the two-cell rates (out of zygotes) were significantly reduced (p<0.05, paired t-test) in the quinKO mice (~39%, n = 67) when compared to the mTmG mice (~88%, n = 58) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M), implying that the quinKO sperm is indeed less efficient in fertilizing eggs and/or supporting early embryonic development, especially the first cleavage of the zygotes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by IVF data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1M.

claim: The two-cell rates were significantly reduced in the quinKO mice (~39%) when compared to the mTmG mice (~88%).
source: Although the blastocyst rate (out of two-cell embryos) of quinKO was comparable to that of the mTmG mice, the two-cell rates (out of zygotes) were significantly reduced (p<0.05, paired t-test) in the quinKO mice (~39%, n = 67) when compared to the mTmG mice (~88%, n = 58) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M), implying that the quinKO sperm is indeed less efficient in fertilizing eggs and/or supporting early embryonic development, especially the first cleavage of the zygotes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by IVF data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1M with statistical analysis.

claim: Comparisons between the KO and WT testes revealed thousands of differentially expressed genes.
source: Comparisons between the KO and WT testes revealed thousands of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (fold change ≥ 2, FDR < 0.05, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 2692, 2028, 1973, 3405, and 1106 DETs were obtained from Mir465 sKO, dKO, tKO, quadKO, and quinKO testes, respectively.
source: We obtained 2692, 2028, 1973, 3405, and 1106 DETs from Mir465 sKO, dKO, tKO, quadKO, and quinKO testes, respectively.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq and target prediction analyses.

claim: GO terms of DETs from each KO testis revealed that the DETs were mostly involved in embryonic development, response to stimulus, centrosome cycle, epithelium morphogenesis, organelle organization, cell projection, RNA metabolic process, and DNA repair.
source: GO terms of DETs from each KO testis revealed that the DETs were mostly involved in embryonic development, response to stimulus, centrosome cycle, epithelium morphogenesis, organelle organization, cell projection, RNA metabolic process, and DNA repair (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The 431 DETs identified to be shared across all five KO testes were also enriched in similar pathways.
source: The 431 DETs identified to be shared across all five KO testes were also enriched in similar pathways (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Crisp1, Egr1, and Trpv4 were significantly downregulated in the quinKO testes.
source: Consistent with the RNA-seq data, qPCR showed that Crisp1, Egr1, and Trpv4 were significantly downregulated in the quinKO testes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by qPCR validation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CRISP1 is downregulated in the quinKO testis when compared to the WT testis.
source: Western blots also confirmed that CRISP1 is downregulated in the quinKO testis when compared to the WT testis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Luciferase assays confirmed that Egr1 and Crisp1 are targets of the MIR-506 family members.
source: Luciferase assays further confirmed that Egr1 and Crisp1 are targets of the MIR-506 family members (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: KO of Crisp1 in mice or inhibition of CRISP1 in human sperm appears to phenocopy the quinKO mice.
source: Of interest, KO of Crisp1 in mice or inhibition of CRISP1 in human sperm appears to phenocopy the quinKO mice (Da Ros et al., 2008; Maldera et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations to previous studies.

claim: Sperm motility in the Crisp1 KO mice is comparable to that in WT mice, but their ability to penetrate the eggs was reduced in the Crisp1 KO mice.
source: Specifically, sperm motility in the Crisp1 KO mice is comparable to that in WT mice, but their ability to penetrate the eggs was reduced in the Crisp1 KO mice (Da Ros et al., 2008); a similar effect was also observed in human sperm treated with anti-hCRISP1 antibody (Maldera et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations to previous studies.

claim: The sRNA-seq data showed that these miRNAs were no longer expressed in the corresponding KOs, confirming the successful deletion of these miRNAs in these KOs.
source: The sRNA-seq data showed that these miRNAs were no longer expressed in the corresponding KOs, confirming the successful deletion of these miRNAs in these KOs (Figure 5C and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In Mir465 sKO testes, miR-201, miR-547, miR-470, miR-471, miR-742, miR-871, miR-881, miR-883a, and miR-883b were all significantly upregulated.
source: Interestingly, in Mir465 sKO testes, miR-201, miR-547, miR-470, miR-471, miR-742, miR-871, miR-881, miR-883a, and miR-883b were all significantly upregulated (FDR <0.05).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: miR-201, miR-547, miR-470, miR-471, miR-871, and miR-883b were all significantly upregulated in the tKO testes.
source: Similarly, miR-201, miR-547, miR-470, miR-471, miR-871, and miR-883b were all significantly upregulated in the tKO testes (FDR < 0.05); miR-201 and miR-547 were all significantly upregulated in the quadKO and the quinKO testes (FDR < 0.05) (Figure 5C and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: miR-201 and miR-547 were all significantly upregulated in the quadKO and the quinKO testes.
source: Similarly, miR-201, miR-547, miR-470, miR-471, miR-871, and miR-883b were all significantly upregulated in the tKO testes (FDR < 0.05); miR-201 and miR-547 were all significantly upregulated in the quadKO and the quinKO testes (FDR < 0.05) (Figure 5C and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Genetic compensation exists among the X-linked MIR-506 family miRNAs.
source: These results support the notion that genetic compensation exists among the X-linked MIR-506 family miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text as a conclusion from the observation that other miRNAs are upregulated when specific clusters are deleted.

claim: Polyandrous mating establishes a situation where sperm from multiple males coexist in the female reproductive tract, with the most competitive ones fertilizing eggs and producing offspring.

claim: IVF may not be ideal for evaluating sperm competition in the real world as it bypasses several key sites where sperm competition likely takes place.

claim: AI may represent a better way to assess sperm competition than IVF, but it is probably less desirable than polyandrous mating.

claim: The MIR-506 family miRNAs share many of their targets and can compensate for each other's absence.
